q.q: Which ABG pattern is typical early in pneumonia?
q.e: Early pneumonia: respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia; severe: respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia.

q.q: Which exam findings indicate consolidation from pneumonia?
o: Increased fremitus, dull percussion and bronchial breath sounds
q.e: Consolidation: ↑ vocal fremitus, dull percussion, bronchial sounds/crackles, whispered pectoriloquy.

q.q: When is BAL indicated in pneumonia per RCP 203?
o: For non-resolving pneumonias and diagnosing bacterial VAP
q.e: RCP 203: BAL for non-resolving pneumonia and as a key tool for bacterial VAP.

q.q: How long after admission must pneumonia develop to be called HAP?
q.e: HAP = ≥ 48 h after admission and not present at admission; VAP uses ≥ 48 h after intubation.
q.src: Pneumonia categories, and typical vs atypical pneumonia

q.q: Which organism is the most common cause of atypical ('walking') pneumonia?
q.e: Mycoplasma is the most common atypical cause; "Atypical pneumonia? → Think macrolide."
q.src: Pneumonia categories, and typical vs atypical pneumonia

q.q: Which describes typical pneumonia?
o: Abrupt rigors, high fever, rusty sputum and lobar consolidation
Flu-like dry cough with diffuse interstitial opacities
No fever and a normal CXR
q.e: Typical (S. pneumoniae): abrupt onset, rigors, purulent/rusty sputum, lobar consolidation.
q.src: Pneumonia categories, and typical vs atypical pneumonia

q.q: What does the RIPE mnemonic check on a chest radiograph?
q.e: Image quality = RIPE: Rotation, Inspiration, Position (AP/PA), Exposure.

q.q: A CXR shows a blunted costophrenic angle. What does this suggest?
q.e: Blunted angle = fluid; flattened diaphragm = hyperinflation.

q.q: Why shouldn't the > 50% cardiothoracic rule be applied to an AP film?
o: The AP view magnifies the heart
The AP view hides the heart
AP films show only the lungs
q.e: Cardiomegaly = heart width > 50% on a PA film; AP magnifies the heart.

q.q: What does an air bronchogram tell you about an opacity?
o: It is in the lung, not the pleura or mediastinum
q.e: Hess: an air bronchogram places the opacity in the lung parenchyma.

q.q: Which pleural effusion is caused by inflammation with increased capillary permeability?
q.e: Exudate: inflammation (infection, malignancy); transudate: systemic pressure changes (CHF most common).

q.q: What is the earliest and most common CXR sign of pleural effusion?
q.e: Blunting appears first; effusions < ~300 mL may not show on a standard CXR.

q.q: How much pleural fluid may be removed during thoracentesis (RCP 203)?
o: All of it, regardless of volume
q.e: Up to ~1500 mL; complications include pneumothorax and re-expansion pulmonary edema.

q.q: Which way does the trachea shift with a large pleural effusion?
q.e: A large effusion pushes the trachea away; fremitus ↓, percussion dull, breath sounds ↓.

q.q: What does accessory muscle use at rest indicate?
q.e: Deck takeaway: accessory muscle use at rest = increased WOB.

q.q: RR 38, accessory muscle use, diaphoresis, falling VT and rising PaCO₂ indicate what?
o: Impending ventilatory failure from muscle fatigue
q.e: NBRC pearl: impending ventilatory failure due to respiratory muscle fatigue.

q.q: Which drug masks accessory muscle use?
q.e: Exam trap: paralysis masks accessory muscle use.

q.q: Which are accessory muscles of inspiration per RCP 203?
o: Sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, upper trapezius, pectoralis major
q.e: Inspiratory accessories: SCM, scalenes, trapezius, pectoralis major (Hess adds external intercostals).

q.q: What minimum NIF does RCP 203 require to extubate?
q.e: RCP 203: a minimum of −20 cm H₂O; the deck range is −20 to −30.

q.q: Which spontaneous VT is the general weaning predictor?
q.e: Use ≥ 5 mL/kg generally; ≥ 4 mL/kg PBW only for the NHLBI ARDS-protocol SBT.

q.q: RR 38 with VT 300 mL. Is the patient ready to wean by RSBI?
q.e: 38 ÷ 0.3 = 127 → not ready.

q.q: During an SBT, which finding is acceptable per RCP 203?
o: PaCO₂ rise ≤ 10 mm Hg with pH ≥ 7.30

q.q: What is the most serious complication of extubation?
q.e: RCP 203 Lssn 6a: laryngospasm is the most serious extubation complication.

q.q: What is a daily sedation interruption also called?
q.e: DSI = sedation vacation = SAT; it allows better assessment of extubation readiness.

q.q: Which peak cough flow means a patient is NOT ready for extubation?
q.e: PCF > 160 normal; 60–160 borderline; < 60 inadequate. The extubation threshold is > 60 L/min.

q.q: Which finding shows the airway can be protected before extubation?
o: A positive gag reflex and ability to raise the head off the bed
q.e: Ready if: patent upper airway, airway protection (gag, head lift), cuff leak, secretion clearance.

q.q: What does the Ch 13 slide say about SIMV for weaning?
o: It is no longer recommended, but you may be tested on it
It is the preferred weaning mode
It must be used for every patient
q.e: "SIMV is no longer recommended" — "but you may be tested on it!"

q.q: How is a conscious patient positioned for thoracentesis?
o: Sitting up, leaning slightly forward over a bedside table
q.e: Conscious: sit up leaning forward; immobile: at the bed edge, affected side down.

q.q: Which chest drainage chamber protects the lung as a one-way valve?
q.e: Water seal (2 cm under water): air leaves but cannot return.

q.q: What sets the amount of suction on a chest drainage system?
o: The water level in the suction-control chamber
How high the wall suction is turned
q.e: 20 cm of water = 20 cm H₂O; turning the wall up only adds bubbling.

q.q: Why might the RT recommend a cough suppressant before thoracentesis?
o: Coughing during the procedure can injure the lung or pleura
q.e: Coughing during the needle insertion can injure the lung or pleura.

q.q: Where are vesicular breath sounds normally heard?
q.e: Vesicular: periphery, soft and low-pitched, inspiration longer than expiration.
q.src: Normal Breath Sounds and Where They Belong

q.q: Bronchial breath sounds are heard over the peripheral lung fields. What do they suggest?
q.e: Dense tissue carries large-airway sound to the chest wall.
q.src: Normal Breath Sounds and Where They Belong

q.q: What does the deck say matters most about a normal breath sound?
o: Its location — a normal sound in the wrong place is abnormal
q.e: Learn the location more than the description.
q.src: Normal Breath Sounds and Where They Belong

q.q: Where are bronchovesicular sounds normally heard?
o: Upper sternum and between the scapulae
q.e: Bronchovesicular: over main bronchi, I = E, moderate pitch.
q.src: Normal Breath Sounds and Where They Belong

q.q: A severe asthmatic's wheezing suddenly stops and breath sounds become very quiet. What does this mean?
o: A silent chest — a late, critical warning of impending arrest
q.e: The silent chest is never improvement; airflow is too low to wheeze.

q.q: Which causes unilaterally diminished breath sounds in a ventilated patient?
q.e: Hess Ch 20: bronchial intubation, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pleural effusion.

q.q: Diminished breath sounds at the bases after surgery commonly mean what?
q.e: Hess: ↓ at the bases is common with postoperative atelectasis.

q.q: What causes fine crackles?
o: Collapsed or fluid-filled small airways and alveoli popping open
q.e: Fine, end-inspiratory crackles: pulmonary edema, ARDS, atelectasis, ILD.

q.q: What is the 'hallmark' lung sound of pulmonary edema?
q.e: Deck: crackles; crackles climbing higher = worsening CHF.

q.q: Coarse crackles over the trachea in an intubated patient indicate what?
o: Retained secretions — an indication to suction
q.e: Hess Box 17-3: coarse crackles over the trachea = suction.

q.q: What sound is classic in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
q.e: Hess Ch 34: bibasilar Velcro-like crackles in IPF.

q.q: What causes a wheeze?
o: Narrowed airways from bronchospasm, edema or mucus
q.e: Wheeze: continuous, musical, from narrowed airways; treat with a bronchodilator.

q.q: A patient develops crowing, high-pitched inspiratory sounds after extubation. What is it and what is given?
q.e: Stridor = upper-airway obstruction (laryngeal edema) → racemic epi.

q.q: Low-pitched, rumbling sounds that change after a cough are what?
o: Rhonchi from secretions in larger airways
q.e: Rhonchi: low-pitched, snoring-like, from secretions; may clear with cough.

q.q: What happens to wheezing in a severe asthma attack?
o: It becomes biphasic — inspiratory and expiratory
q.e: Severe asthma: wheezing heard on both inspiration and expiration.

q.q: What does a pleural friction rub sound like and why?
o: A grating, leather-like sound from inflamed pleural surfaces
A crowing sound from the larynx
q.e: Inflamed pleura no longer glide; localized, may be intermittent.
q.src: Pleural Friction Rub, Grunting and Voice Sounds

q.q: Why do newborns in respiratory distress grunt?
o: They close the glottis to maintain lung volume
q.e: Hess: grunting maintains lung volume by expiring against a closed glottis.
q.src: Pleural Friction Rub, Grunting and Voice Sounds

q.q: When a patient says 'e' and it sounds like 'a' over the lung, what is this?
q.e: Voice sounds get louder and clearer over consolidation.
q.src: Pleural Friction Rub, Grunting and Voice Sounds

q.q: Which findings fit a pneumothorax?
o: Absent breath sounds, trachea away, hyperresonance
q.e: Pneumothorax: absent sounds, tracheal shift away, hyperresonant.

q.q: Which findings fit atelectasis?
o: Diminished sounds, trachea toward the affected side, dullness
q.e: Atelectasis pulls the trachea toward the collapse; dull percussion.

q.q: Which breath sounds does Hess give for emphysema?
o: Decreased or absent, with no adventitious sounds
q.e: Hess Table 1-3: emphysema = decreased or absent, no adventitious sounds.

q.q: What is orthopnea?
o: Difficult breathing when lying down, relieved by sitting up
q.e: Orthopnea: uncomfortable breathing when lying down, relieved by sitting/standing.

q.q: Why does lying flat worsen breathing in CHF?
o: Venous return increases and fluid redistributes into the lungs
q.e: Supine: blood shifts centrally, filling pressures rise, interstitial edema forms.

q.q: How can orthopnea be assessed at the bedside?
o: Ask how many pillows the patient sleeps on
q.e: Hess: orthopnea may be hidden in a patient sleeping on two or three pillows.

q.q: How soon after falling asleep does paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea wake the patient (exam answer)?
q.e: Use 1–2 hours; PND commonly suggests cardiac dysfunction.

q.q: What is platypnea?
q.e: Hess: platypnea is the opposite of orthopnea.

q.q: Which pattern is deep and fast, regular, without apnea, and caused by metabolic acidosis?
q.e: Kussmaul: compensatory hyperventilation for DKA or severe metabolic acidosis.

q.q: Which pattern waxes and wanes in a crescendo–decrescendo cycle with apnea?
q.e: Cheyne-Stokes: CHF, stroke, brain injury, central sleep apnea.

q.q: Which pattern has irregular breaths of equal tidal volume followed by apnea?
q.e: Biot's: CNS injury, ↑ ICP, brainstem damage, meningitis.

q.q: How do Biot's and Cheyne-Stokes breathing differ?
o: Biot's breaths are equal in size; Cheyne-Stokes breaths build and fade
Cheyne-Stokes is caused only by DKA
q.e: Biot's points to brainstem involvement and more severe neurologic dysfunction.

q.q: For the exam, how is Kussmaul breathing described?
q.e: Use the deck's deep and fast (Hess Ch 4's 'normal or reduced frequency' is the outlier).

q.q: Why does Kussmaul breathing occur?
o: To blow off CO₂ and compensate for metabolic acidosis
q.e: Expelling CO₂ reduces acid; in the DKA case the compensation is only partial.

q.q: What causes Cheyne-Stokes breathing in CHF?
o: Delayed circulation time makes the brain respond to CO₂ changes too late
q.e: The brain keeps overcorrecting because the CO₂ signal arrives late.

q.q: How common is Cheyne-Stokes breathing in CHF patients (Hess)?
q.e: Hess Ch 45: CSB in 25–40% of CHF patients; treat by improving cardiac function.

q.q: Which way does the trachea shift with atelectasis?
q.e: "Toward loss / Away from pressure": volume loss pulls the trachea.
q.src: Tracheal shift: which way, and what causes it

q.q: Which conditions push the trachea away from the affected side?
o: Tension pneumothorax and large pleural effusion
q.e: Space-occupying processes push the trachea away.
q.src: Tracheal shift: which way, and what causes it

q.q: How is tracheal position checked at the bedside?
o: Index finger at the sternal notch, moved gently side to side
With a stethoscope over the heart
q.e: RCP 103: the trachea is normally midline above the sternal notch.
q.src: Tracheal shift: which way, and what causes it

q.q: Why shouldn't you wait for tracheal deviation to treat a suspected tension pneumothorax?
o: It is a late and unreliable finding
It appears first in every case
q.e: Treat based on distress, unilateral ↓ sounds and instability.
q.src: Tracheal shift: which way, and what causes it

q.q: What is paradoxical breathing?
o: The chest or abdomen moves in on inhalation and out on exhalation
q.e: It signals respiratory distress and high WOB.

q.q: The abdomen moves inward on inspiration. What does this suggest?
q.e: Hess: abdominal paradox = diaphragm weakness; chest wall paradox = chest wall muscle paralysis or flail.

q.q: Thoracoabdominal paradox appears during an SBT. What should be done?
q.e: Paradox is an early sign of weaning failure.

q.q: How does the deck define flail chest?
o: Three or more ribs fractured in two or more places, a sternal fracture or costochondral separation
One rib fractured in one place
q.e: Use the deck's three or more (Hess says two or more).

q.q: How does a flail segment move?
o: In on inspiration and out on exhalation
Out on inspiration and in on exhalation
q.e: Negative intrapleural pressure draws the segment in on inspiration.

q.q: Why can a pulmonary contusion with flail chest worsen?
o: It always resolves in an hour
q.e: Contusions worsen over 24–48 h; consider early elective intubation.

q.q: Does every flail chest patient need intubation?
o: No — treat with pain control, hygiene and O₂, ventilating when necessary
Only if a rib is broken
q.e: Not every flail patient needs intubation or MV.

q.q: How does a tension pneumothorax differ from a simple one?
o: Tension compromises both breathing and circulation
q.e: One-way valve → rising pressure → ↓ venous return → obstructive shock.

q.q: On volume control, what ventilator sign suggests a tension pneumothorax?
o: A sudden increase in airway pressure
q.e: VC: sudden ↑ pressure; PC: sudden ↓ VT.

q.q: What should be recommended when tension pneumothorax is suspected and life-threatening?
o: Immediate needle decompression or a chest tube
q.e: Also 100% O₂ and lower PIP/VT if on PPV.

q.q: Why does 100% O₂ help a small pneumothorax resolve?
o: It washes out nitrogen, speeding reabsorption of pleural air
q.e: Nitrogen washout lowers pleural gas pressure; no substitute for decompression under tension.

q.q: Where is a needle thoracostomy performed per the Ch 15 deck?
q.e: Insert over the top of the third rib; then prepare for a chest tube.

q.q: What is attached to the angiocath after needle decompression?
q.e: A Heimlich valve is a one-way valve; its arrow points away from the patient.

q.q: Which patients are predisposed to tension pneumothorax?
o: Patients on MV with airway pressures over 40–45 cm H₂O
Patients with normal lungs at rest
q.e: Also chest trauma and very high compliance (advanced emphysema).

q.q: Which CXR findings fit a tension pneumothorax?
o: Hyperlucent pleural space, collapsed lung, mediastinal shift to the opposite side
q.e: Also flattened diaphragm and widened rib spaces on the affected side.

q.q: Using the Ch 15 deck, which heart rate triggers a rapid response call?
q.e: Deck: HR < 40 or > 130 (Hess: > 140).
q.src: The Ch 15 Deck’s MET / RRT Activation Criteria

q.q: Using the Ch 15 deck, which respiratory rate triggers a rapid response call?
q.e: Deck: RR < 8 or > 30 (Hess: > 28).
q.src: The Ch 15 Deck’s MET / RRT Activation Criteria

q.q: Which SpO₂ triggers a MET call in the Ch 15 deck?
q.e: Deck: SpO₂ < 90% (Hess: < 89% despite O₂).
q.src: The Ch 15 Deck’s MET / RRT Activation Criteria

q.q: Which urine output triggers a rapid response call?
q.e: Both sources agree: < 50 mL over 4 hours.
q.src: The Ch 15 Deck’s MET / RRT Activation Criteria

q.q: Which systolic BP triggers a call in the Ch 15 deck?
q.e: Deck: SBP < 90 (no high-BP trigger); Hess adds > 180.
q.src: The Ch 15 Deck’s MET / RRT Activation Criteria

q.q: Which interventions do RTs commonly perform on a MET call?
o: Suctioning, FiO₂ changes, NIV, bronchodilators, ABGs and intubation
q.e: Ch 15: suctioning, FiO₂, NIV, bronchodilators, ABG monitoring, intubation, transport.
q.src: The Ch 15 Deck’s MET / RRT Activation Criteria

q.q: Can a staff member call the RRT for concern alone, with normal vital signs?
o: Yes — significant staff concern is a valid trigger
No — vital signs must be abnormal
q.e: Exam trap: staff concern alone is a valid trigger.
q.src: Vital signs and findings that trigger a Rapid Response Team call

q.q: In the Hess model criteria, which mental status finding triggers a call?
q.e: Any acute change in mental status triggers an RRT call.
q.src: Vital signs and findings that trigger a Rapid Response Team call

q.q: What is the goal of a rapid response team?
o: Intervene in the pre-arrest period to prevent ICU transfer, arrest or death
q.e: Hess: RRTs intervene during the critical pre-arrest period.
q.src: What the RRT is and who is on it

q.q: Which patients are at highest risk of needing an RRT call?
o: Postop patients in the first 12–24 hours and patients just transferred out of the ICU
Patients on room air with normal vitals
q.e: Also: nighttime activation is associated with higher mortality.
q.src: What the RRT is and who is on it

q.q: Who is on the RRT in Hess Table 28-5?
o: A critical care nurse, a respiratory therapist and a physician backup
q.e: Hess calls the RT "a valuable member of the rapid response team."
q.src: What the RRT is and who is on it

q.q: A serious adverse effect occurs during therapy. What is the triple-S rule?
o: Stop the therapy, Stay with the patient, Stabilize with O₂ and help
Send for help, Sit down, Sign the chart
q.e: Stop, Stay, Stabilize — then notify nurse and physician.
q.src: When to Stop a Therapy — the Triple-S Rule

q.q: During a treatment, SpO₂ falls by 5%. What should the RT do?
o: Stop the therapy — a > 4% drop is a reason to stop
q.e: A > 4% SpO₂ drop or any fall below 90% is an adverse effect.
q.src: When to Stop a Therapy — the Triple-S Rule

q.q: What are the two reasons to stop or recommend discontinuing a therapy?
o: The patient is in jeopardy, or the goals have been achieved
The order expired or the patient refused once
Low supplies or a busy unit
q.e: Ch 13: safety in jeopardy, or therapy goals achieved.
q.src: When to Stop a Therapy — the Triple-S Rule

q.q: How do mL and cc compare?
o: They are exactly the same volume
q.e: 3 mL = 3 cc.

q.q: How many grams are in 4,500 mg?
q.e: 1,000 mg = 1 g; move the decimal 3 places.

q.q: How many mL are in one tablespoon?
q.e: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 tbsp = 15 mL; 1 cup = 240 mL.

q.q: A 1.5-kg infant needs caffeine citrate 20 mg/kg as a loading dose. What is the dose?
q.e: 20 mg/kg × 1.5 kg = 30 mg.
q.src: The Proportion Method and mg/kg Dosing

q.q: What is the first step in the proportion method?
q.e: First convert to consistent units, then set Known Dose/Known Amount = Desired Dose/Desired Amount.
q.src: The Proportion Method and mg/kg Dosing

q.q: What is the beractant (Survanta) dose in the decks?
q.e: Beractant 4 mg/kg birth weight; poractant 2.5 mL/kg (max 5 mL/kg).
q.src: The Proportion Method and mg/kg Dosing

q.q: How do you convert a percent-strength solution to mg/mL?
How many mg of albuterol are in 3 mL of a 0.083% solution?
How many mL of 0.5% albuterol give 2.5 mg?
How much drug is in 0.5 mL of 2.25% racemic epinephrine?
What is the most common mistake in percent-solution problems?
o: Forgetting to convert the % to mg/mL first
q.e: Trap: forgetting to convert %, or mixing up mg (weight) and mL (volume).

q.q: 2.5 mg of albuterol is mixed with 5 mL of saline instead of 2 mL. What changes?
o: Only the treatment time — the dose is the same
q.e: Diluent changes only the time to deliver; "more saline = weaker treatment" is wrong.
q.src: Diluent Does Not Change the Dose

q.q: Why is diluent added to small-volume nebulizer drugs?
o: Most nebulizers don't aerosolize well below about 1 mL of dead volume
q.e: Aim for about 2.5–3 mL total so the nebulizer works efficiently.
q.src: Diluent Does Not Change the Dose

q.q: How much drug is in a 1:1000 solution?
q.src: Ratio Solutions, w/w – w/v – v/v, and Diluting a Stock Solution

q.q: How much 20% stock is needed to make 5 mL of a 10% solution?
o: 2.5 mL of stock plus 2.5 mL water
1 mL of stock plus 4 mL water
q.e: V₁ × C₁ = V₂ × C₂ → x × 20 = 5 × 10 → x = 2.5 mL.
q.src: Ratio Solutions, w/w – w/v – v/v, and Diluting a Stock Solution

q.q: How many ppm equal 1%?

q.q: How does acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) reduce mucus viscosity?
o: Its free sulfhydryl groups break disulfide bonds in mucoproteins
It kills bacteria in the mucus
q.e: NAC substitutes free thiol groups for disulfide bonds connecting mucin proteins.

q.q: What is the most important hazard of aerosolized acetylcysteine?
q.e: Bronchospasm (less with 10%), nausea, rotten-egg odor, mechanical obstruction; give a bronchodilator first.

q.q: What is acetylcysteine's most important use today?
o: Antidote for acetaminophen overdose to protect the liver
q.e: "NAC saves the liver!" — very testable. Routine aerosolized NAC for airway clearance is not recommended.

q.q: What is the critical rule about neuromuscular blocking agents?
o: They do not sedate or relieve pain — give analgesia, then sedation, then the paralytic
q.e: "Paralysis ≠ sedation"; order: analgesia → sedation → paralytic, and the patient must be ventilated.

q.q: Which is the only depolarizing neuromuscular blocker?
q.e: Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing NMBA; it causes fasciculations first.

q.q: What is the most important complication of succinylcholine?
q.e: "If you remember ONE complication" — hyperkalemia; caution in burns, trauma, denervation.

q.q: What is the difference between sedation and analgesia?
o: Sedation diminishes awareness; analgesia relieves pain
Sedation relieves pain; analgesia causes sleep
q.e: "Sedative ≠ Analgesic": propofol/midazolam sedate; morphine/fentanyl relieve pain.

q.q: Which sedative gives sedation, anxiolysis and some analgesia without respiratory depression?
q.e: Dexmedetomidine, a selective α₂ agonist; it can be continued through extubation.

q.q: Why is propofol called 'milk of amnesia', and what must be watched?
o: It is a lipid emulsion; watch for hypotension and rising triglycerides
It is a water solution; watch for hypertension
It is a gas; watch for fire
It is a pill; watch for nausea
q.e: Propofol is a lipid emulsion (adds calories, raises triglycerides); watch BP, apnea, bradycardia.

q.q: What does the deck call the #1 thing opioids can kill?
q.e: Respiratory depression is the most important opioid side effect.

q.q: What reverses opioids?
q.e: Naloxone, which also comes as a nasal spray; withdrawal may appear within minutes in dependent patients.

q.q: How much stronger is hydromorphone (Dilaudid) than morphine?
q.e: Hydromorphone is 5–10× stronger than morphine.

q.q: What is a drug's plasma half-life?
o: The time for plasma concentration to fall by one-half
The time to reach peak effect
q.e: T½ = time for the plasma concentration to decrease by one-half.

q.q: Why are older adults and patients with liver or kidney disease at greater risk of drug toxicity?
o: Drug half-lives are longer in these conditions
q.e: Hess: half-lives are longer with age and hepatic or renal impairment.

q.q: Which drug has an extremely short half-life of about 12 seconds?
q.e: Adenosine ~12 seconds ("super short").

q.q: Which route is 'parenteral'?
q.e: Parenteral = any route other than enteral (IV, IM, SubQ, IO, IT).

q.q: Which is an advantage of the inhaled route?
o: Smaller dose with fewer side effects and rapid onset
q.e: Inhaled: smaller dose, fewer side effects, rapid onset, targets the lungs, painless.

q.q: Why must nondepolarizing NMBAs be given IV?
o: They are poorly absorbed in the GI tract
They need the liver to activate
q.e: Nondepolarizing NMBAs are poorly absorbed orally, so IV only.

q.q: What does bioavailability indicate?
o: The proportion of a drug that reaches the systemic circulation
How fast a drug is eliminated
q.e: IV is the standard at 100% bioavailability.

q.q: What does high first-pass metabolism do to an oral drug?
q.e: The liver inactivates much of the drug before it reaches the circulation.

q.q: Which practice raises the lung/total (L/T) ratio of an inhaled drug?
o: Mouth rinsing and a breath hold
q.e: Higher L/T = more efficient lung delivery: efficient devices, reservoirs, rinse and spit, breath hold, instruction.

q.q: What are the major organs of drug elimination (Hess)?
o: The kidney and, to a lesser extent, the liver
q.e: Kidney and liver are major; lungs, saliva and sweat are minor routes.

q.q: What primarily determines how quickly drugs are eliminated?
o: Renal function measured by creatinine clearance or eGFR
q.e: Elimination depends primarily on renal function (CrCl or eGFR).

q.q: According to Chang's memory line, where are benzodiazepines metabolized and excreted?
q.e: "Liver = Metabolism, Kidneys = Excretion."

q.q: Which is more specific for kidney function?
q.e: Creatinine (from muscle) is filtered with little reabsorption; BUN reflects protein metabolism and hydration.

q.q: What is the normal BUN range in the RCP 202 Renal deck?
q.e: BUN 7–20 mg/dL; creatinine men 0.7–1.3, women 0.6–1.1.

q.q: A patient has a high BUN with a normal creatinine. What does this suggest?
q.e: High BUN with normal creatinine → dehydration or high protein; both high → kidney disease/AKI.

q.q: What is beclomethasone (QVAR)?
o: An inhaled corticosteroid controller, not a rescue agent
q.e: ICS: maintenance control of chronic asthma; not for acute severe asthma.

q.q: What are the most common side effects of inhaled corticosteroids?
q.e: Prevent with the minimal dose, a reservoir, and rinsing the mouth.

q.q: How do inhaled steroids interact with β-agonists?
o: They restore β-responsiveness by increasing β-receptors
They replace β-agonists in acute attacks
q.e: Steroids increase the number and availability of β-receptors.

q.q: What is the onset and duration of a SABA per the class slide?
q.e: Use the class slide's 4–6 hours for albuterol and levalbuterol.

q.q: How does levalbuterol differ from albuterol?
q.e: Albuterol is 50:50 R and S; levalbuterol is pure R (less tremor/HR, superiority unproven).

q.q: What is the standard albuterol nebulizer dose (RCP 103)?
q.e: RCP 103 Asthma: 2.5 mg/3 mL NS.

q.q: Which is a side effect of β-agonists?
q.e: β-agonist effects: tremor, ↑ HR, tolerance, ↓ K⁺, ↑ glucose, paradoxical bronchospasm.

q.q: What class of drug is ipratropium (Atrovent)?
q.e: Hess: a short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA).

q.q: What is the most common side effect of ipratropium?
q.e: Also cough and mydriasis (protect the eyes); cardiac changes not usually seen.

q.q: Why does ipratropium stay mostly in the lungs?
o: As a quaternary ammonium compound it crosses lipid membranes poorly
It is absorbed only by mucus
It is too large to inhale
q.e: It does not distribute well across lipid membranes.

q.q: What is the deck's ipratropium MDI dose?
q.e: Deck: MDI 17 µg × 2 puffs QID; SVN 0.5 mg QID.

q.q: How do LABAs differ from SABAs?
o: LABAs are controllers lasting 12–24 h; SABAs are rescue drugs lasting 4–6 h
q.e: LABA onset ~20 min, duration 12–24 h; lipophilic.

q.q: Can a LABA be used alone in asthma?
o: No — always with an inhaled corticosteroid, and never for rescue
q.e: LABAs may mask inflammation; combine with ICS.

q.q: Which is a long-acting β₂-agonist?
q.e: LABAs: salmeterol, formoterol, arformoterol; ultra-LABAs indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol.

q.q: How does montelukast work?
o: It blocks the CysLT1 leukotriene receptor
q.e: Montelukast: receptor antagonist; zileuton blocks production via 5-LO.

q.q: Which antileukotriene requires liver-function monitoring?
q.e: Zileuton inhibits 5-LO; monitor liver function; interacts with theophylline and warfarin.

q.q: Are leukotriene inhibitors used for acute asthma attacks?
q.e: They protect against exercise-, aspirin- and allergen-induced asthma; effective in ~50–70%.

q.q: Which immunoglobulin is the 'asthma antibody' that attaches to mast cells?
q.e: IgE triggers allergic reactions; IgA protects mucosa; IgG most common; IgM first responder.

q.q: How does omalizumab (Xolair) work?
o: It binds IgE, blocking its attachment to mast cells
q.e: Omalizumab for allergic (IgE) asthma, SC every 2–4 weeks.

q.q: Which biologics block interleukin-5 for eosinophilic asthma?
q.e: Anti-IL-5 reduces eosinophils.

q.q: What does palivizumab (Synagis) prevent?
q.e: For BPD, prematurity < 35 weeks, congenital heart disease; 15 mg/kg IM monthly in season.

q.q: What is the most severe side effect of monoclonal antibody biologics?
q.e: Biologics are add-ons, not for acute relief and not a replacement for ICS.

q.q: How often is tiotropium (LAMA) given?
q.e: Deck: tiotropium and umeclidinium once daily; aclidinium bid.
q.src: Standard Dosing Frequency and Sites of Action

q.q: How is tobramycin (TOBI) dosed?
o: 300 mg BID, 28 days on / 28 days off
q.e: Deck: TOBI 300 mg BID on alternating 28-day cycles.
q.src: Standard Dosing Frequency and Sites of Action

q.q: What is the dornase alfa dose and mechanism?
o: 2.5 mg daily; breaks down DNA in secretions
5 mg BID; thins mucus by osmosis
q.e: Dornase alfa: 2.5 mg daily.
q.src: Standard Dosing Frequency and Sites of Action

q.q: Which receptor mediates bronchodilation?
q.e: β₁ heart, β₂ lungs, α₁ vasoconstriction, M3 airway smooth muscle constriction.
q.src: Standard Dosing Frequency and Sites of Action

q.q: What is the recommended order for multiple inhaled medications?
o: Bronchodilator → mucolytic → airway clearance → steroid → antibiotic
q.e: Open the airway, thin and clear secretions, then deliver steroid and antibiotic.

q.q: For which patient should an SVN be reserved?
o: Acutely ill adults who cannot use a DPI or MDI
q.e: Infants: MDI with holding chamber and mask; outpatient adults: DPI if flow is adequate.

q.q: In an acute asthma exacerbation, how often is the SABA repeated?
o: Every 20 minutes up to 3 times, or continuous nebulization
q.e: Ch 12 deck.

q.q: When are aerosolized antibiotics such as TOBI or Cayston generally indicated?
q.e: Generally only CF with suspected or confirmed Pseudomonas.

q.q: How is an emergency drug given down the ETT?
o: 2–2.5× the IV dose, diluted in 10 mL, followed by 5–10 rapid inflations
The same as the IV dose, undiluted
q.e: LEAN drugs; patient supine, compressions halted, catheter past the ETT tip.

q.q: How is surfactant instilled?
o: Through a catheter up to, not past, the ETT tip, split between each dependent bronchus
q.e: Confirm ETT position by CXR first; avoid suctioning for 6 hours if possible.

q.q: Is prophylactic or rescue surfactant recommended for infants under 30 weeks?
q.e: Prophylactic reduces pneumothorax, PIE and neonatal mortality.

q.q: How does albuterol lower serum potassium?
o: β₂ stimulation increases Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, moving K⁺ into cells
It makes the kidneys excrete K⁺
It binds K⁺ in the gut
It removes K⁺ through the lungs
q.e: Total body K⁺ is unchanged — a bridge therapy that can rebound.

q.q: What albuterol dose is used for hyperkalemia?
q.e: Far above the bronchodilator dose; lowers K⁺ ~0.5–1.0 mEq/L.

q.q: What is the RASS target for moderate sedation?
q.e: RASS runs +4 (combative) to −5 (unarousable); 0 = alert and calm.

q.q: What principle permits comfort dosing that may hasten death during withdrawal of life support?
q.e: Relief must be the intent; raising doses to hasten death is euthanasia.

q.q: Before withdrawing life support, which drugs should be stopped?
o: Paralytics and drugs that don't add comfort
q.e: Comfort comes from analgesia and sedation; FiO₂ is lowered to 30% first.

q.q: In the 40-50-60 / 70-80-90 rule, what SpO₂ corresponds to a PaO₂ of 50 torr?
q.src: The Rule and How to Use It

q.q: An SpO₂ of 70% suggests about what PaO₂?
q.e: The rule applies when SpO₂ is below 90%.
q.src: The Rule and How to Use It

q.q: When does RCP 203 say the 40-50-60 rule applies?
q.e: It is approximate ("about equal").
q.src: The Rule and How to Use It

q.q: Why is the 60/90 pair important?
o: It is the threshold for hypoxemia and supplemental O₂
It is the CO poisoning cutoff
It is the ventilator weaning ceiling
q.e: Hypoxemia = PaO₂ < 60 or SaO₂ < 90% on room air.

q.q: At what saturation does central cyanosis first appear with normal Hb?
q.e: Near the rule's 80/50 pair.

q.q: How accurate are pulse oximeters with good perfusion?
q.e: They also overestimate saturation when HbCO is present.

q.q: What air:O₂ ratio gives an FiO₂ of 40%?
What air:O₂ ratio gives an FiO₂ of 60%?
What air:O₂ ratio gives 28% in Hess Table 14-2?
How is total flow from an air-entrainment device calculated?
q.e: Total parts = air parts + 1.
q.src: Step 2: Total Flow = O₂ Flow × Total Ratio Parts

q.q: A 40% device runs at 10 L/min. What is the total flow?
q.e: 3:1 → 4 parts × 10 = 40 L/min.
q.src: Step 2: Total Flow = O₂ Flow × Total Ratio Parts

q.q: The same 40% device is turned down to 5 L/min. What changes?
o: Total flow falls to 20 L/min; FiO₂ stays 40%
q.e: Changing O₂ flow changes only total flow, not the ratio.
q.src: Step 2: Total Flow = O₂ Flow × Total Ratio Parts

q.q: As the set FiO₂ rises on an entrainment device, what happens to total flow?
q.e: Higher FiO₂ → less air entrained → lower total flow.
q.src: Step 2: Total Flow = O₂ Flow × Total Ratio Parts

q.q: What total flow does the deck target for an air-entrainment device?
q.e: The device is high-flow only if it meets the patient's inspiratory flow.
q.src: Matching Total Flow to the Patient

q.q: How much O₂ flow is needed for a 60% device to deliver 40 L/min?
q.src: Matching Total Flow to the Patient

q.q: What minimum flow does Hess give relative to minute ventilation?
q.e: About 40 L/min for adults.
q.src: Matching Total Flow to the Patient

q.q: How can you tell a patient is out-breathing an aerosol entrainment device?
o: The mist disappears from the mask or T-piece during inspiration
q.e: FiO₂ then falls and the system becomes low-flow.
q.src: Matching Total Flow to the Patient

q.q: What should be used for FiO₂ > 0.60 at flows > 40 L/min?
q.e: The deck says use a blender.
q.src: Matching Total Flow to the Patient

q.q: Why do the decks say to 'learn how the mode works — not just the name'?
o: Mode names are not standardized between manufacturers
Every ventilator uses the same mode names
q.e: Names are manufacturer-dependent (e.g. PRVC on Servo = VC+ on PB840 = AutoFlow on Dräger).
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: According to the golden rule, how many variables can a ventilator control at once?
q.e: Control volume and pressure varies; control pressure and volume varies.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: A breath is triggered by the patient but cycled by the ventilator. How is it classified?
q.e: "If the patient controls both = Spontaneous. If the ventilator controls either one = it's Mandatory."
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: In volume control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: VT stays the same and pressure increases
VT falls and pressure stays the same
q.e: VC guarantees VT; pressure is the dependent variable and rises as compliance falls.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: In pressure control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: Pressure stays the same and VT decreases
VT stays the same and pressure rises
q.e: PC guarantees pressure; VT falls with decreased compliance.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: PC is set at 20 cm H₂O with PEEP 10 cm H₂O. What is the PIP?
q.e: PIP = pressure control + PEEP = 20 + 10 = 30 cm H₂O.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: What is the key difference between the control mode (CMV) and assist/control?
o: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; CMV (control) does not
CMV allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths
q.e: The slide's one-line difference: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; control mode does not.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: A/C is set at 12 breaths/min and the patient triggers 24. How many full breaths are delivered?
q.e: In A/C every triggered breath gets the full preset support; the set rate is a minimum.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: How is a patient-triggered (assisted) breath identified on the pressure waveform?
o: A negative deflection below baseline before inspiration
A sudden drop in PEEP to zero
q.e: Assist = negative deflection before inspiration; time-triggered control breaths have none.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: What problem does IMV (unsynchronized) cause that SIMV avoids?
q.e: IMV can deliver a mandatory breath before a spontaneous one is exhaled → breath stacking, auto-PEEP.

q.q: In SIMV with PS 8, which breaths receive the pressure support?
o: Only the spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths
No breaths — PS is inactive in SIMV
q.e: PS applies only to spontaneous breaths; mandatory breaths deliver the preset VT.

q.q: Why is SIMV usually combined with pressure support?
o: To prevent muscle fatigue and high WOB on spontaneous breaths
To guarantee VT on every breath
q.e: Without PS, SIMV can cause muscle fatigue and weaning failure; PS helps the spontaneous breaths.

q.q: How is pressure support classified?
q.e: PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — a phrase on NBRC-style exams repeatedly.

q.q: When does a pressure-supported breath end?
o: When inspiratory flow falls to a preset percentage of peak flow, often ~25%
When the preset VT is reached
q.e: PS breaths flow-cycle, often at about 25% of peak flow.

q.q: Why can PSV not be used alone in an apneic patient?
o: Every PS breath must be patient-triggered
q.e: PS is active only on spontaneous breaths, so it needs an intact respiratory drive.

q.q: How does MMV ensure adequate ventilation?
o: It increases mandatory breaths when spontaneous V̇E falls below a preset minimum
It guarantees VT on every breath
q.e: MMV is a "minimum ventilation safety net": low V̇E → more volume-cycled mandatory breaths.

q.q: On MMV with a target of 8 L/min, the patient breathes 9 L/min alone. What does the ventilator do?
q.e: If the patient breathes enough, MMV stays out of the way.

q.q: What does MMV NOT guarantee?
o: That every breath has an adequate VT
q.e: MMV guarantees minimum total V̇E, not an adequate VT on every breath.

q.q: Which mode automatically adjusts inspiratory pressure to maintain a target VT while minimizing airway pressure?
q.e: Board pearl: PRVC delivers the target VT at the lowest PIP possible.

q.q: On PRVC, the patient's compliance worsens. What does the ventilator do?
o: Raises the inspiratory pressure to deliver the target VT
q.e: Compliance worsens → PRVC raises pressure; compliance improves → it lowers pressure.

q.q: On Automode, the patient makes two consecutive patient-triggered breaths. What happens?
o: It switches from PRVC to Volume Support
It switches to CPAP with no support
q.e: Automode: sleeping patient → PRVC; awake patient (two triggered breaths) → Volume Support.

q.q: What is Volume Control Plus (VC+) on the PB 840?
q.e: VC+ = PB's PRVC: preset VT and I-time with variable pressure and flow.

q.q: How does Volume Support differ from pressure support?
o: VS guarantees volume and lets pressure vary; PS guarantees pressure and lets volume vary
VS is time-cycled; PS is flow-cycled
VS needs a set rate; PS does not
q.e: Both are patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled; VS targets volume.

q.q: On Volume Support, the patient makes more effort. What happens to the support pressure?
q.e: Less effort → higher PS; more effort → lower PS, to hold the target VT.

q.q: What does PAV target?
o: No set flow, volume or pressure — support is proportional to the patient's effort
q.e: "With PAV there is no target flow, volume, or pressure"; pull harder → more assist.

q.q: What happens if the PAV % assist is set too high?
q.e: Too high → runaway; too low → excessive patient WOB.

q.q: Which patient is NOT suitable for PAV?
o: An apneic patient with no respiratory drive
q.e: PAV requires intact drive and a functional neuromuscular system.

q.q: How is APRV defined in the decks?
o: Inverse ratio, pressure-controlled IMV with unrestricted spontaneous breathing
q.e: APRV: inverse ratio, pressure-controlled, intermittent mandatory ventilation with unrestricted spontaneous breathing.

q.q: Which settings are used in APRV?
o: FiO₂, Phigh, Plow, Thigh and Tlow
Amplitude, Hz and mean airway pressure
q.e: APRV has no VT or rate setting; Thigh and Tlow set the release frequency.

q.q: How long does an adult spend at Plow during APRV (Hess)?
q.e: Tlow 0.2–0.8 s; 80–95% of the cycle is at Phigh, producing intrinsic PEEP.

q.q: On HFOV, how is CO₂ removal improved?
o: Increase the amplitude or decrease the frequency (Hz)
q.e: ↓ Hz → larger oscillatory VT → ↑ CO₂ removal — "backwards from conventional ventilation."

q.q: On HFOV, how is oxygenation improved?
o: Increase the mean airway pressure or FiO₂
q.e: Oxygenation: ↑ mean airway pressure or ↑ FiO₂.

q.q: How does HFOV exhalation differ from conventional ventilation?
o: Exhalation is active — the oscillator pulls gas out
q.e: HFOV actively pushes gas in and pulls it out; conventional exhalation is passive.

q.q: Which mode gives a target VT at the lowest PIP with pressure auto-adjusted breath to breath?
q.e: Side-by-side table: PRVC = target VT at lowest PIP, pressure auto-adjusted.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: Which mode is listed as historical and not offered on new adult ventilators?
q.e: IMV causes breath stacking; all current ventilators offer SIMV instead.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: What is patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: The ventilator's breath delivery is out of phase with the patient's effort
The patient's heart rate is irregular
q.e: Hess: synchrony = breath delivery in phase with patient effort; asynchrony = out of phase.

q.q: Which is a consequence of patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: Increased WOB and sedation needs, and longer ventilation
q.e: Asynchrony decreases comfort, increases WOB and sedation needs, and prolongs ventilation.

q.q: A COPD patient's respiratory rate is higher than the ventilator's measured rate. What is the likely cause?
o: Auto-PEEP preventing some efforts from triggering
q.e: Patient rate > ventilator rate means efforts are missed, commonly from auto-PEEP raising the trigger threshold.

q.q: During VC, a vigorous patient effort pulls the pressure waveform downward and PIP varies breath to breath. What is the problem?
q.e: The ventilator isn't meeting inspiratory flow demand; fix by raising flow or switching to PC/PS.

q.q: A pressure dip early in inspiration on the waveform suggests what?
o: Inadequate peak flow — 'I need more flow'
q.e: Early dip = "I need more flow"; late dip = "I want more volume."

q.q: A patient receives a second breath almost immediately after the first, nearly doubling the set VT. What is this?
q.e: Premature cycling: the patient's effort continues after the breath ends and double-triggers.

q.q: What is the recommended order for fixing asynchrony?
o: Adjust settings → reconsider the mode → sedation/analgesia → neuromuscular blockade last
Change the mode first, then sedate
q.e: Troubleshoot and adjust settings first; "Paralytics don't fix problems — they hide them."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What does Hess call a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator?
q.e: "Anxiety is a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: Why can SIMV itself cause mode asynchrony?
o: The respiratory center cannot adapt to the varying breath types
q.e: Mode asynchrony occurs when the ventilator delivers different breath types, as in SIMV.
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What is normal adult inspiratory flow per the Principles deck?
q.e: Principles deck: normal adult inspiratory flow = 40–60 L/min.

q.q: With constant flow of 60 L/min for 1 second, what tidal volume is delivered?
q.e: 60 L/min = 1 L/s; VT = flow × TI = 1 L.

q.q: What are the three control variables per the Principles deck?
q.e: Control variables: volume, pressure and time; trigger/limit/cycle are phase variables.

q.q: What is the 'independent variable' on a ventilator?
q.e: "Whatever the ventilator guarantees is called the independent variable"; the other floats.

q.q: In PC, which change increases the delivered VT?
q.e: Box 20-5: VT rises with ↑ driving pressure, longer TI (while flow present) and more effort.

q.q: In VC, which change raises PIP?
q.e: Box 20-4: PIP rises with ↑ flow, constant flow, ↑ PEEP, auto-PEEP, ↑ VT, ↑ Raw, ↓ compliance.

q.q: What starts a time-triggered breath?
q.e: Rate 12 → a breath every 5 s; time-triggered breaths show no negative deflection.

q.q: Base flow is 10 L/min and flow sensitivity is 3 L/min. When does the ventilator trigger?
o: When expiratory-circuit flow drops to 7 L/min
q.e: Hess's example: it triggers at 7 L/min, assuming the patient inhaled 3 L/min.

q.q: A trigger set at −5 cm H₂O is too insensitive. What results?
o: The patient may not be able to trigger and fatigues
q.e: Too high (not sensitive enough) → can't trigger; too sensitive (−0.5) → auto-trigger.

q.q: According to the deck's memory line, how is pressure control cycled?
q.e: "Volume Control is volume-cycled. Pressure Control is time-cycled. PSV is flow-cycled."

q.q: When does pressure cycling most often occur?
o: As an alarm condition when the high-pressure limit is reached
q.e: Pressure cycling most often occurs as a high-pressure alarm condition (e.g. a cough during VC).

q.q: How is Volume Support classified (trigger/limit/cycle)?
q.e: VS: patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — like PS but volume-targeted.

q.q: What is the number one ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation?
q.e: Pearl: PEEP is primarily an oxygenation intervention, not a ventilation intervention.
q.src: PEEP: What It Is, What It Does, How Much

q.q: How does PEEP improve oxygenation?
o: It keeps alveoli open at end-expiration, increasing FRC and reducing shunt
q.e: PEEP prevents end-expiratory collapse → ↑ FRC → ↑ V/Q → better oxygenation.
q.src: PEEP: What It Is, What It Does, How Much

q.q: What is CPAP?
o: PEEP applied to a patient breathing entirely on their own
q.e: CPAP = PEEP with all spontaneous breaths; on BiPAP, EPAP = PEEP.
q.src: PEEP: What It Is, What It Does, How Much

q.q: What PEEP level is associated with an increased incidence of barotrauma?
q.e: "PEEP > 10 (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50) is associated with increased alveolar rupture or barotrauma."
q.src: PEEP Complications and the Dangerous Level

q.q: What is the major downside of PEEP?
o: Decreased venous return, cardiac output and blood pressure
q.e: ↑ PEEP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP.
q.src: PEEP Complications and the Dangerous Level

q.q: How can PEEP raise ICP?
o: Higher intrathoracic pressure impedes venous drainage from the brain
q.e: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, impeding cerebral venous drainage.
q.src: PEEP Complications and the Dangerous Level

q.q: What is auto-PEEP?
o: Unintentional PEEP from gas trapped because exhalation did not finish before the next breath
q.e: Auto-PEEP (intrinsic, inadvertent, occult PEEP) = trapped gas; total PEEP = set PEEP + auto-PEEP.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP detected on the flow–time waveform?
o: Expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath
There is a negative deflection before every breath
q.e: Expiratory flow failing to reach baseline before the next breath = air trapping.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP measured?
o: An end-expiratory pause; pause pressure minus set PEEP
An end-inspiratory pause; Pplat minus PEEP
q.e: Occlude just before the next breath; e.g. 12 − 5 = 7 cm H₂O auto-PEEP. The patient must be relaxed.

q.q: What does PIP overcome, compared with plateau pressure?
o: PIP overcomes resistance and compliance; Pplat overcomes compliance only
PIP overcomes compliance only; Pplat overcomes resistance
q.e: Pplat is measured with no flow, so it excludes airway resistance; PIP − Pplat = flow × resistance.

q.q: PIP rises from 25 to 40 cm H₂O while Pplat stays at 20. What is the likely cause?
o: Increased airway resistance, such as secretions or bronchospasm
q.e: "When only PIP moves, think airways."

q.q: PIP and Pplat both rise by 10 cm H₂O. What is the likely cause?
o: Decreased compliance, such as pulmonary edema or pneumothorax
q.e: "When PIP and Plateau move together, think lungs."

q.q: According to Hess, what is the most important ventilator alarm?
q.e: Hess: the patient-disconnect alarm — a low-pressure and/or low exhaled volume alarm.

q.q: Expired VT is lower than set VT on every breath and PIP is lower than before. What is the problem?
q.e: A leak is low on every breath; with air trapping, expired VT is low for 2–3 breaths, then high.

q.q: The low PEEP alarm sounds. What is the usual cause?
o: A leak in the circuit or ETT cuff
q.e: "Failure of the circuit to hold PEEP is usually due to leakage in the circuit or ETT cuff."

q.q: Which circuit type is used on noninvasive ventilators?
o: Single-limb without an exhalation valve (a leak port)
Single-limb with a mushroom valve only
q.e: NIV uses a known leak port; the ventilator calculates and subtracts the leak.

q.q: Where is the exhalation valve in a double-limb (wye) ICU circuit?
q.e: Double-limb circuits carry exhaled gas back to the ventilator's expiratory/PEEP valve.

q.q: Circuit compliance is 3 mL/cm H₂O, PIP 60 and PEEP 10. How much volume is compressed in the circuit?
q.e: 3 mL/cm H₂O × (60 − 10) = 150 mL; corrected VT = expired VT − 150 mL.

q.q: What are the two jobs of the exhalation valve?
o: Separate inspiration from expiration and set PEEP
Warm the gas and measure VT
q.e: Closed in inspiration, open for exhalation; the expiratory valve controls PEEP.

q.q: Which circuit obstruction is the more serious?
o: Expiratory obstruction — it can cause rebreathing, asphyxia or barotrauma
q.e: Expiratory obstruction is more serious; it comes with low-volume and high-pressure alarms.

q.q: Why must the expiratory valve be checked during aerosolized ribavirin?
o: Ribavirin can crystallize and occlude valves and sensors
q.e: Ribavirin crystals impair expiratory valves and sensors; watch for ↑ peak pressures.

q.q: What does the equation of motion describe?
o: The pressure needed to deliver a breath to overcome airway resistance and lung/chest wall elastance
The relationship between FiO₂ and PaO₂
q.e: Pressure must overcome R × flow (resistive load) and E × volume (elastic load).

q.q: In the equation of motion, what is elastance?
q.e: E = respiratory system elastance (lungs + chest wall), the inverse of compliance.

q.q: During full ventilatory support, what is Pmus in the equation of motion?
o: Zero — all pressure comes from the ventilator
q.e: Full support: Pmus = 0. Spontaneous breathing: Paw = 0. Partial: both contribute.

q.q: Which four ventilator modes does the Ch 11 deck say to 'KNOW THESE' for the NBRC?
q.e: Control variable (volume or pressure) × A/C or SIMV; PS and PEEP are add-ons.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: According to the Ch 11 deck, what are the three categories of patient–ventilator asynchrony?
q.e: Use the deck's trigger, flow, cycle (Hess says trigger, cycle, mode).

q.q: How is adult HFOV weaned per the Ch 11 deck?
o: FiO₂ to 0.40 first, then lower mean airway pressure 2–3 cm H₂O every 4–6 h to ≤ 20, then switch to PC
q.e: Then consider PC (limit ≤ 30, PEEP 10–12) and a standard SBT.

q.q: Where does the Ch 11 deck set the high-pressure alarm before PIP is measured?
o: 35 cm H₂O, then 10 above the observed PIP once stable
q.e: Ch 11 (AARC): 35 initially, then 10 above observed PIP.

q.q: Where does the Ch 11 deck set the low inspiratory pressure alarm?
o: 10 cm H₂O below the observed PIP (or the set pressure in PC)
q.e: With the low VT alarm (150 mL above and below set VT), it detects leaks or disconnection.

q.q: The volume–time curve does not return to baseline. What does the Ch 11 deck say this means?
o: A leak — often the ETT cuff
q.e: Likely on the NBRC: find the leak (cuff, connections, humidifier, mask, chest tube/BPF).

q.q: How is static compliance calculated, and what pressure is ignored?
q.e: Ch 11: in a static-compliance table, disregard PIP — "it is there to confuse you."

q.q: VT 600 mL, Pplat 27, PEEP 10, PIP 40. What is the static compliance?
q.e: 600 ÷ (27 − 10) = 35.3; PIP is a distractor.

q.q: What normal static compliance does RCP 203 give for intubated adults?
q.e: Use RCP 203's 40–80; < 25–30 → ↑ WOB and weaning difficulty.

q.q: How does dynamic compliance compare with static compliance?
o: It is always less, the difference being airway resistance
q.e: Cdyn = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP); PIP includes resistive pressure.

q.q: How is alveolar ventilation calculated?
q.e: V̇A accounts for dead space; V̇E = VT × f does not.

q.q: A 125-lb patient breathes 15/min with VT 400 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
How does lowering VT affect VD/VT?
o: It raises VD/VT and lowers alveolar ventilation

q.q: How much water vapor does fully saturated gas hold at 37 °C?
Condensate is visible in the inspiratory tubing near the patient. What does this indicate?
o: The gas is fully saturated (100% RH)
The temperature is too low to matter
q.e: No visible condensate = RH could be anywhere 0–99%.

q.q: How should circuit condensate be handled?
o: Drained with gloves away from the patient and discarded as contaminated waste
q.e: Never let it reach the airway; never return it to the reservoir.

q.q: What humidity does an HME provide per the deck?
q.e: Heated humidifier: near 100% RH at body temperature; HME 70–90% at 30–31 °C.

q.q: What happens if cuff pressure is too high?
o: Tracheal mucosal ischemia, ulceration and necrosis
q.e: Too high (> 25–30) obstructs mucosal blood flow; too low (< 20) allows aspiration.

q.q: A cuff needs more than 30 cm H₂O to seal. What does this suggest?
o: The tube may be too small — evaluate and recommend exchange
The cuff is overinflated on purpose
q.e: Rising pressures over time suggest tracheal dilation or cuff/pilot balloon malfunction.

q.q: Is the minimal leak technique recommended for cuff management?
o: No — it is no longer recommended
q.e: RCP 203 and the VAP strategies: avoid the minimal leak technique.

q.q: What pressure is the King LT cuff inflated to?
q.e: ETT 20–30; LMA ≤ 60; King LT ~60 cm H₂O.

q.q: Rate 15, VT 600 mL, and the physician orders I:E 1:4. What inspiratory flow is needed?
q.e: V̇E 9 L/min ÷ %I-time 0.20 = 45 L/min.

q.q: What %I-time corresponds to an I:E ratio of 1:2?
A ventilated COPD patient has auto-PEEP with an I:E of 1:2. What should be done?
o: Decrease the ratio toward 1:4 or 1:5 by lengthening E-time
q.e: Severe obstruction needs long E-times; lowering the rate lengthens E-time.

q.q: What is the permissive hypercapnia floor in the Ch 13 deck?
o: pH below 7.25–7.30 — then raise the rate or give bicarbonate
q.e: pH is the stop sign, not PaCO₂.

q.q: What must be programmed into the ventilator to use automatic tube compensation (ATC)?
o: The patient's airway type and size
q.e: ATC dynamically offsets tube resistance for spontaneous breaths.

q.q: In the ARDSNet protocol, what VT is used at the start and the target?
o: Start 8 mL/kg PBW; reduce by 1 mL/kg to 6 mL/kg
q.e: Reduce 1 mL/kg at intervals ≤ 2 h until VT = 6 mL/kg PBW.
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: In ARDSNet, what is done if Pplat exceeds 30 cm H₂O?
o: Decrease VT in 1 mL/kg steps to a minimum of 4 mL/kg
q.e: Pplat ≤ 30; measure every 4 h and after each PEEP or VT change.
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: In ARDSNet, the pH is 7.10 with the rate already at 35. What is done?
o: Increase VT in 1 mL/kg steps until pH > 7.15; consider NaHCO₃
q.e: For pH < 7.15, raise rate to 35 first; then VT (Pplat may be exceeded).
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: What pH goal does the ARDSNet protocol use?
q.e: pH goal 7.30–7.45; PaO₂ 55–80 or SpO₂ 88–95%.
q.src: The ARDSNet Protocol Step by Step (Ch 14)

q.q: What does a recruitment maneuver do?
o: Briefly raises transpulmonary pressure to reopen collapsed alveoli
q.e: Recruitment opens; adequate PEEP afterward keeps alveoli open.

q.q: Are recruitment maneuvers routinely recommended in ARDS per the revised Ch 11 deck?
o: No — lung-protective ventilation, PEEP and proning come first
q.e: Better oxygenation does not guarantee a better outcome.

q.q: How is decremental PEEP titration done after a recruitment maneuver?
o: Lower PEEP in small steps, then set it slightly above where compliance starts to fall
Raise PEEP until the BP drops
q.e: In the deck's example, PEEP was chosen at 18 cm H₂O.

q.q: When should a recruitment maneuver be stopped?
o: If MAP falls below 60–65 mm Hg or the patient deteriorates
q.e: Do RMs only in hemodynamically stable patients (MAP ≥ 65).

q.q: Is there a sourced 'normal' range for adult PIP?
o: No — sources give only ceilings, such as 'safe' < 50 cm H₂O
q.e: Only ceilings exist; Pplat is the one to watch (< 30).
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What Pplat ceiling should be used for this exam?
q.e: Conflict: Chang prints < 35; use < 30 (ARDSNet, Hess, Ch 11).
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What low-level PEEP is often used to prevent atelectasis in ventilated patients (Hess)?
q.e: Initial PEEP 5 (NBRC range 2–6); 'safe' < 10.
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What normal airway resistance does RCP 203 give for intubated adults?
q.e: RCP 203 intubated normals: Crs 40–80 mL/cm H₂O, Raw 5–12 cm H₂O/L/s.
q.src: Normal (Target) Levels of PIP, Pplat and PEEP

q.q: What does PIP − Pplat represent?
q.e: Depends on flow setting and airway resistance.

q.q: Which pressure is used for the < 15 cm H₂O lung-protective driving-pressure limit?
q.e: In PC, VT is changed via ΔP = PIP − PEEP (Ch 11), but the < 15 limit is Pplat − PEEP.

q.q: Why does Pplat reflect only compliance?
o: It is measured during an end-inspiratory hold with no flow
It is measured during peak flow
q.e: No flow means no resistive pressure.

q.q: PIP rises while Pplat stays normal. What is the lung condition?
q.e: Bronchospasm, secretions, edema, water in circuit, kinked ETT.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: PIP and Pplat rise together. Which is a likely cause?
q.e: ↓ compliance (stiff lungs): ARDS, edema, pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, mainstem intubation.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: PIP is lower than the previous breath on every breath, but pressure returns to baseline. What is it?
q.e: A leak lowers PIP every breath.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: In pressure control, how does a stiffer lung show up?
q.e: Pressure is fixed in PC, so worse mechanics reduce VT.
q.src: Lung Condition When PIP and Pplat Rise or Fall

q.q: What happens with too little PEEP?
o: Alveoli collapse, causing shunt and poor oxygenation
q.e: Too little → collapse; too much → overdistension, barotrauma, ↓ CO.
q.src: PEEP Too Low vs Too High

q.q: What does the Ch 11 deck call optimal PEEP?
o: The PEEP that keeps SpO₂ ≥ 88–90% without lowering BP
q.e: Optimal PEEP balances oxygenation against hemodynamics.
q.src: PEEP Too Low vs Too High

q.q: Is PEEP > 10 cm H₂O an absolute ceiling?
o: No — it is Chang's barotrauma risk threshold; ARDS may need more
q.e: Ch 11's optimal-PEEP examples are 15 and 18.
q.src: PEEP Too Low vs Too High

q.q: How does raised intrathoracic pressure lower urine output?
o: Reduced cardiac output lowers renal blood flow, and ADH rises
q.e: PPV → ↓ CO → ↓ renal flow; ↑ ADH and ↓ ANP retain fluid.
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: Why can CVP rise with PEEP even though preload is falling?
o: Intrathoracic pressure raises the measured CVP while venous return falls
q.e: "High CVP does not always mean lots of preload."
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: Which organ is hit first by falling cardiac output from PPV?
q.e: The kidneys are more sensitive than the liver; hepatic perfusion falls only when PEEP is added.
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: How can PPV benefit a patient with left heart failure?
q.e: Hess: the drop in LV afterload can help fluid overload or LV failure.
q.src: Effects on the Body When Pressures Rise

q.q: How does the deck define auto-PEEP in the pressures topic?
o: Residual alveolar pressure at end-exhalation from air trapping
q.e: Aka occult/intrinsic PEEP, dynamic hyperinflation; common in COPD and asthma.
q.src: Auto-PEEP: What It Is and How to Find It

q.q: End-expiratory pause pressure is 12 with set PEEP 5. What is the auto-PEEP?
q.e: Auto-PEEP = pause pressure − set PEEP.
q.src: Auto-PEEP: What It Is and How to Find It

q.q: Which graphic does the Ch 11 deck say is likely on the NBRC for auto-PEEP?
o: Expiratory flow not returning to zero before the next breath
Volume curve not returning to baseline
q.e: Volume not returning to baseline = a leak; flow not returning to zero = air trapping.
q.src: Auto-PEEP: What It Is and How to Find It

q.q: Which change does NOT help resolve auto-PEEP?
q.e: Fixes lengthen expiratory time: ↓ RR, ↑ flow, ↓ VT, ↓ TI, bronchodilators.

q.q: How much extrinsic PEEP may be applied to counter auto-PEEP per RCP 203?
o: Up to 80–90% of measured auto-PEEP, in spontaneously breathing patients
q.e: Use RCP 203's 80–90% (Hess: 75–85%); it helps patients trigger.

q.q: Which axes does a pressure–volume loop use?
o: Pressure on the x-axis, volume on the y-axis
Volume on the x-axis, flow on the y-axis
Flow on the x-axis, pressure on the y-axis
q.e: The P-V loop is the "compliance" loop.
q.src: The Pressure-Volume (P-V) Loop: How to Read It

q.q: What does the slope of the static P-V curve represent?
q.e: Ch 11: "the higher the slope, the higher the compliance."
q.src: The Pressure-Volume (P-V) Loop: How to Read It

q.q: How does a spontaneous breath look on a P-V loop?
o: Oval and symmetric with no sharp corners
A small trigger dip then machine assistance
q.e: Controlled = sharp angles; assisted = small trigger effort, then assistance.
q.src: The Pressure-Volume (P-V) Loop: How to Read It

q.q: Compliance decreases. How does the P-V loop shift?
o: Toward the pressure axis (right) and flatter
Toward the volume axis (left) and steeper
q.e: ↓ compliance: ↑ PIP and ↑ PAlv; ARDS, edema, atelectasis, fibrosis.
q.src: Compliance Changes on the P-V Loop

q.q: Which condition shifts the P-V loop toward the volume axis (steeper)?
q.e: Emphysema has high compliance with poor recoil.
q.src: Compliance Changes on the P-V Loop

q.q: What does PEEP or surfactant do to the P-V curve when compliance improves?
q.e: Improved compliance → steeper curve.
q.src: Compliance Changes on the P-V Loop

q.q: What does a 'beak' (duckbill) at the top of the P-V loop indicate?
q.e: Beyond the UIP, small volume rises cause large pressure rises; reduce VT.

q.q: What is the lower inflection point?
o: The pressure where alveoli begin to open (critical opening pressure)
q.e: Below it the curve is flat (under-recruitment).

q.q: Where does Ch 11 set PEEP relative to the lower inflection point?
q.e: Optimal PEEP = the lowest pressure that exceeds the LIP.

q.q: How is overdistension on the P-V loop fixed?
o: Reduce VT until the beak disappears
q.e: Or use pressure control.

q.q: On the P-V loop, what does a wider loop indicate (exam answer)?
q.e: Use "wider = more resistance" (slide 74 notes; RCP 203 Ch 4).

q.q: On which scalar does Ch 11 show a leak?
o: Volume–time: exhaled volume doesn't return to baseline
Flow–time: flow doesn't return to zero
q.e: Flow not returning to zero = auto-PEEP; volume not returning = leak.

q.q: What is the normal work of breathing range that both books share?
q.e: Hess 0.3–0.7, Heuer 0.5–0.7 J/L; 0.5–0.7 is the overlap.

q.q: Which loop should you 'think resistance' for?
q.e: "Volume/Pressure Loop = compliance; Flow/Volume Loop = resistance."

q.q: On a ventilator flow–volume loop, what does bronchospasm do to the expiratory limb?
o: Lowers peak expiratory flow and makes the limb flatter
q.e: Inspiratory flow is preset; look at the expiratory limb.

q.q: How is bronchodilator response seen on a flow–volume loop?
o: Peak expiratory flow improves after the bronchodilator
q.e: Ch 11 Fig 11-10: compare before and after.

q.q: Which spirometry flow–volume shape fits obstruction?
o: A concave ('scooped') expiratory curve, L-shaped when severe
q.e: Obstructive: concave downward; restrictive: tall narrow 'ice cream cone'.

q.q: Flow is reduced equally on inspiration and expiration. What does this suggest?
o: Fixed upper-airway obstruction such as tracheal stenosis
q.e: A variable lesion (vocal cord paralysis) reduces flow only on forced inhalation.

q.q: Which spirometry loop shape is restrictive?
o: An 'upside-down ice cream cone' with rapid emptying
q.e: Hess Ch 8.

q.q: Which setting does RCP 105 say controls CO₂?
q.e: "Rate controls CO₂. FiO₂ and PEEP control oxygenation."

q.q: A ventilated patient has respiratory acidosis. What does RCP 203 say to change first?
q.e: ↑ rate first; if that fails, ↑ VT within 4–8 mL/kg PBW and Pplat ≤ 30.

q.q: Will raising the FiO₂ lower a high PaCO₂?
q.e: Exam trap: raising FiO₂ does not lower PaCO₂.

q.q: A COPD patient on the ventilator has PaCO₂ 55 and pH 7.37. What should be done?
o: Nothing to drive the PaCO₂ to 40 — the pH is normal
Increase the rate to bring PaCO₂ to 40
q.e: In chronic CO₂ retention a normal pH can come with PaCO₂ ≥ 55; don't force it to 40.

q.q: Rate, VT and Pplat are at their limits and the pH is still below 7.30. What does RCP 203 allow?
q.e: Let PaCO₂ rise as long as pH stays > 7.20–7.25.

q.q: Set rate 14, PaCO₂ 60, desired PaCO₂ 40. What is the new rate?
q.src: Calculating the new rate for a target PaCO₂

q.q: Why does raising the rate lower PaCO₂?
o: PaCO₂ varies inversely with alveolar ventilation
Rate lowers dead space to zero
q.e: With constant CO₂ production, ↑ V̇E lowers PaCO₂.
q.src: Calculating the new rate for a target PaCO₂

q.q: What is the risk of setting a very high rate in COPD?
o: Shortened expiratory time causing air trapping and auto-PEEP
q.e: Too high a rate shortens TE → air trapping and auto-PEEP.
q.src: Calculating the new rate for a target PaCO₂

q.q: A ventilated patient has a low PaCO₂ compensating for diabetic ketoacidosis. What should be done?
o: Reduce the rate to normalize PaCO₂
q.e: A compensatory PaCO₂ must not be normalized.
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: A patient's PaCO₂ drops because they are hypoxic. What is the correct action?
o: Fix the hypoxia first; don't reduce ventilation
q.e: Low PaCO₂ as a response to hypoxia: fix the hypoxia.
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: An ABG shows metabolic acidosis on the ventilator. What ventilator change is indicated?
o: None — don't increase support for a metabolic problem
q.e: No ventilator adjustment for metabolic disorders; treat the cause.
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 50 from oversedation. What does the deck say?
o: Find and correct the cause; increasing the rate is not the proper action
q.e: For high PaCO₂ from oversedation or fatigue, correct the cause (e.g. delay weaning).
q.src: When the ABG says change the vent but you should not

q.q: Oxygenation is acceptable on less than 50% O₂. What should be adjusted to fine-tune it?
q.e: RCP 203: if acceptable on < 50% O₂, adjust FiO₂; if not, adjust PEEP.
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: As oxygenation improves, which is lowered first?
q.e: Lower FiO₂ to ≤ 0.50 first, then PEEP.
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: What FiO₂ ceiling should be used to avoid O₂ toxicity on this exam?
q.e: Conflict resolved: use < 50% (RCP 105 Initiation, and RCP 203's switch point).
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: What PaO₂/SpO₂ goals apply in ARDS lung-protective ventilation?
q.e: ARDSNet goals: PaO₂ 55–80, SpO₂ 88–95%.
q.src: Oxygenation targets, FiO₂ limits, FiO₂ vs PEEP

q.q: A BiPAP patient on 10/5 needs better ventilation only. What is the NBRC change?
q.e: Ventilation only → ↑ IPAP, so ΔP rises and baseline stays.

q.q: A BiPAP patient on 10/5 needs better oxygenation and ventilation. What is the change?
q.e: Both → raise both, IPAP more than EPAP.

q.q: On BiPAP, which pressures adjust oxygenation?
q.e: Ventilation via IPAP/ΔP; oxygenation via FiO₂/EPAP.

q.q: PEEP 10 with FiO₂ 75% and PaO₂ 130. Which should be lowered first?
o: FiO₂ — oxygen toxicity is the concern
q.e: Lower whichever is more dangerous: high FiO₂ → oxygen toxicity.

q.q: PEEP 18 with FiO₂ 45% and PaO₂ 120. Which should be lowered first?
q.e: High PEEP with modest FiO₂ → PEEP is the concern.

q.q: PaO₂ 52 on FiO₂ 0.70. What does the 60-60 rule say?
q.e: PaO₂ < 60 on FiO₂ > 0.6 = shunt → PEEP/CPAP.

q.q: PaO₂ 55 on FiO₂ 0.35. What is the likely mechanism and fix?
q.e: FiO₂ below 0.6 → V/Q imbalance responds to a simple FiO₂ increase.

q.q: When VT is properly set (6–8 mL/kg PBW, Pplat < 30), what is preferred to change V̇E?
q.e: RR changes are the preferred method once VT is set correctly.
